NEW ORLEANS, Louisiana (CNN) -- A grand jury has indicted four people in the shooting death of a woman during what police say was a Ku Klux Klan initiation rite in the Louisiana woods, St. Tammany Parish prosecutors said. Raymond "Chuck" Foster is reputed to be the leader of the Klan Group. He was among the four indicted. Raymond "Chuck" Foster, 44, was indicted on second-degree murder charges Wednesday in the November death of Cynthia Lynch, 43, of Tulsa, Oklahoma. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, said Rick Wood, spokesman for the St. Tammany Parish district attorney's office. "That's what he was charged with," Wood told reporters on Wednesday. "The grand jury agreed with that charge." Two other men, including Foster's son, Shane Foster, were indicted on a count of obstruction of justice, and a woman, Danielle Jones, was indicted on one count of being an accessory after the fact. Wood said Thursday Foster's case was assigned to one judge and the others' cases were assigned to another. Foster is scheduled to be arraigned March 3, he said, and the others are set for arraignment next week. Eight people initially were arrested in the case. The remaining four were not indicted. "Haven't seen one like this," Wood said Wednesday. "We've had a lot of high-profile cases, but not one like this. ... As (district attorney) Walter Reed said, it will be to the max. They will be prosecuted to the max." Authorities said Lynch was recruited over the Internet and took a bus to Slidell, Louisiana, where she was met by two Klan members. They then went to a campsite in the woods near Sun, Louisiana, about 60 miles north of New Orleans, where they met other members of the group, police said. During the initiation rite, members of the Klan group, which calls itself the Sons of Dixie, shaved Lynch's head, according to Capt. George Bonnett of the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff's Department and Sheriff Jack Strain, who spoke to CNN in November. After 24 hours of drills, including chanting and running with torches, she asked to be taken to town. An argument began, authorities said, and the group's leader, Raymond Foster, pushed Lynch to the ground and shot her without warning. Lynch apparently wanted to leave because she was homesick, investigators found after talking to her family members. After the shooting, "Foster, we believe, removed a knife from his pocket and rolled over the victim and began a process of trying to remove the bullet from her body ... because he was trying to destroy evidence where law enforcement would not be able to piece these things together," Strain said. Police believe other members of the Sons of Dixie helped cover up the slaying on Foster's behalf, Strain said at the time, including burning some of Lynch's personal items. "We're up to the challenge," Wood told reporters after the indictments were handed up Wednesday. "This office is ready to proceed and take care of business." Authorities received the initial tip about the slaying from a convenience store clerk, after two group members went into the store and asked him if he knew how to get bloodstains out of their clothes. The clerk told them he did not, then called police after they left. Officials tracked down those two members and arrested them, then arrested others at the campsite and Foster. All the members surrendered without incident, police said. Investigators found Confederate battle flags, Ku Klux Klan banners, five Klan robes and an Imperial Wizard robe at the campsite, authorities said. Lynch's body was found under loose brush along a road several miles from the campsite. Raymond Foster has a history of Ku Klux Klan activity dating back seven years, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center, a Montgomery, Alabama-based organization that tracks hate groups.

**NEW ORLEANS, Louisiana (CNN) —** A grand jury has indicted four people in connection with the shooting death of a woman during what police described as a Ku Klux Klan initiation ritual in the Louisiana woods, according to St. Tammany Parish prosecutors.

Raymond “Chuck” Foster, the reputed leader of the Klan group, was among those indicted. Foster, 44, was charged Wednesday with second-degree murder in the November death of Cynthia Lynch, 43, of Tulsa, Oklahoma.

If convicted, Foster faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, said Rick Wood, spokesman for the St. Tammany Parish District Attorney’s Office.

“That’s what he was charged with,” Wood told reporters Wednesday. “The grand jury agreed with that charge.”

Two other men, including Foster’s son, Shane Foster, were indicted on one count each of obstruction of justice. A woman, Danielle Jones, was indicted on one count of being an accessory after the fact.

Wood said Thursday that Foster’s case had been assigned to one judge, while the other defendants’ cases had been assigned to another. Foster is scheduled to be arraigned March 3, and the others are set to be arraigned next week, he said.

Eight people were initially arrested in the case. The remaining four were not indicted.

“Haven’t seen one like this,” Wood said Wednesday. “We’ve had a lot of high-profile cases, but not one like this. ... As [District Attorney] Walter Reed said, it will be to the max. They will be prosecuted to the max.”

Authorities said Lynch was recruited over the Internet and traveled by bus to Slidell, Louisiana, where she was met by two Klan members. They then went to a campsite in the woods near Sun, Louisiana, about 60 miles north of New Orleans, where they met other members of the group, police said.

During the initiation ritual, members of the Klan group, which calls itself the Sons of Dixie, shaved Lynch’s head, according to Capt. George Bonnett of the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Department and Sheriff Jack Strain, who spoke to CNN in November.

After 24 hours of drills, including chanting and running with torches, Lynch asked to be taken into town. An argument ensued, authorities said, and the group’s leader, Raymond Foster, pushed Lynch to the ground and shot her without warning.

Investigators determined, after speaking with Lynch’s family members, that she apparently wanted to leave because she was homesick.

After the shooting, “Foster, we believe, removed a knife from his pocket and rolled over the victim and began a process of trying to remove the bullet from her body ... because he was trying to destroy evidence where law enforcement would not be able to piece these things together,” Strain said.

Police believe other members of the Sons of Dixie helped conceal the killing on Foster’s behalf, Strain said at the time, including by burning some of Lynch’s personal belongings.

“We’re up to the challenge,” Wood told reporters after the indictments were handed up Wednesday. “This office is ready to proceed and take care of business.”

Authorities received the initial tip about the killing from a convenience store clerk after two group members entered the store and asked whether he knew how to remove bloodstains from their clothing. The clerk said he did not, then called police after they left.

Officials tracked down and arrested the two members, then arrested Foster and others at the campsite. All surrendered without incident, police said.

Investigators found Confederate battle flags, Ku Klux Klan banners, five Klan robes and an Imperial Wizard robe at the campsite, authorities said. Lynch’s body was discovered beneath loose brush along a road several miles from the campsite.

According to the Southern Poverty Law Center, a Montgomery, Alabama-based organization that monitors hate groups, Raymond Foster has a history of Ku Klux Klan activity dating back seven years.

NEW ORLEANS, Louisiana (CNN) — Prosecutors in St. Tammany Parish said a grand jury indicted four people in connection with the fatal shooting of a woman during what authorities described as a Ku Klux Klan initiation ceremony in a wooded area of Louisiana.

Among those charged was Raymond “Chuck” Foster, the reputed leader of the Klan organization. Foster, 44, was indicted Wednesday on a charge of second-degree murder in the November killing of Cynthia Lynch, a 43-year-old Tulsa, Oklahoma, resident.

Rick Wood, a spokesman for the St. Tammany Parish district attorney’s office, said Foster could receive up to life in prison if found guilty.

“That’s what he was charged with,” Wood told reporters Wednesday. “The grand jury agreed with that charge.”

Two additional men—including Foster’s son, Shane Foster—were each indicted on an obstruction-of-justice count. Danielle Jones was charged with one count of being an accessory after the fact.

Wood said Thursday that Foster’s prosecution had been assigned to one judge, while another judge would handle the cases against the other defendants. Foster’s arraignment was scheduled for March 3, and the remaining defendants were expected to be arraigned the following week.

Authorities originally arrested eight people, but the grand jury declined to indict the other four.

Wood said Wednesday that the case was unlike any he had encountered. Although the office had handled numerous prominent cases, he said, none had resembled this one. Quoting District Attorney Walter Reed, Wood added that the defendants would be prosecuted “to the max.”

Investigators said Lynch was contacted through the Internet and traveled by bus to Slidell, Louisiana. Two Klan members met her there and took her to a wooded campsite near Sun, Louisiana, approximately 60 miles north of New Orleans. Police said other members of the organization were waiting at the site.

The group called itself the Sons of Dixie. During Lynch’s initiation, members shaved her head, Capt. George Bonnett of the St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Department and Sheriff Jack Strain told CNN in November.

After spending 24 hours participating in drills—including chanting and running while carrying torches—Lynch asked to be taken into town. Authorities said an argument followed, during which Raymond Foster, the group’s leader, knocked Lynch to the ground and shot her without warning.

Based on conversations with Lynch’s relatives, investigators concluded that she apparently wanted to leave because she was homesick.

Strain said investigators believed that, after the shooting, Foster took a knife from his pocket, turned Lynch’s body over and attempted to extract the bullet. According to Strain, Foster was trying to eliminate evidence and prevent law enforcement officers from reconstructing what had happened.

Police also suspected that other Sons of Dixie members assisted Foster in concealing the killing. Strain said at the time that those efforts included setting fire to some of Lynch’s belongings.

Following the indictments Wednesday, Wood told reporters that his office was prepared to handle the prosecution and was ready for the challenge.

The investigation began after a convenience-store employee alerted authorities. Two members of the group had entered the store and asked the clerk whether he knew how to remove bloodstains from clothing. The employee said he did not, but contacted police after the pair departed.

Officials located and arrested those two individuals, then detained Foster and other group members at the campsite. Police said everyone surrendered peacefully.

At the campsite, investigators discovered Confederate battle flags, Ku Klux Klan banners, five Klan robes and a robe identifying its wearer as an Imperial Wizard.

Lynch’s body was recovered several miles from the campsite. It had been placed beneath loosely arranged brush beside a road.

According to the Southern Poverty Law Center, a Montgomery, Alabama-based organization that monitors hate groups, Raymond Foster had been involved in Ku Klux Klan activity for seven years.

The city is also considered the birthplace of jazz, with live performances filling clubs, restaurants, and public spaces throughout the year.

New Orleans is perhaps best known for Mardi Gras, an annual celebration featuring elaborate parades, costumes, music, and community traditions.
